lines.text:
Under the Waves — Life on Board a Submarine

A submarine is a vessel that travels beneath the surface of the ocean. It can stay underwater for weeks or even months. Life inside is cramped, noisy, and fascinating.

The outside of the submarine is called the hull — a strong metal shell designed to resist the enormous pressure of deep water. The conning tower rises from the top of the hull and contains the periscope — a tube with mirrors that allows the crew to see the surface while the submarine stays hidden below. A hatch on top provides the only way in or out. Portholes — small, round windows — are found on some older submarines. At the back, a propeller pushes the vessel through the water, and a rudder steers it left or right.

To dive, the submarine fills its ballast tanks with water, making it heavier than the surrounding sea. To rise, compressed air pushes the water out, making the submarine lighter. This simple principle — controlling weight — is how a submarine moves up and down. A torpedo tube is built into the bow for military submarines. A sonar dome on the front sends sound waves through the water to detect objects.

Inside the submarine, the control room is the centre of operations. A navigation screen shows the submarine's position. A depth gauge tells the crew how far below the surface they are. A compass shows direction. A radar screen and a sonar display help the crew detect other vessels. The helm — a steering wheel — controls direction. A throttle controls speed. A communication radio connects the crew to the surface. An alarm warns of danger.

The captain commands the submarine from the control room. A navigator plots the course using a sea chart and GPS. An engineer maintains the engines and systems. A sonar operator listens for sounds in the water. A radio operator handles communications. A technician repairs equipment. A cook prepares meals in the galley — the submarine's small kitchen. A medic provides medical care. A diver may be on board for special missions. The first officer is second in command.

Living spaces are tight. Crew members sleep in bunk beds stacked three high. The mess hall is where everyone eats — and the only social space. A storage locker holds personal items. The bathroom and shower are shared. A small laundry handles uniforms. A library and a recreation room provide entertainment during long patrols.

The ocean outside is monitored constantly. A depth meter tracks the submarine's depth. A buoy can be released to mark a position. An anchor holds the submarine in place when surfaced. A searchlight illuminates the dark water. An underwater camera records images. An echo sounder maps the ocean floor. A current meter measures the movement of the water.

Life on a submarine requires discipline, teamwork, and the ability to live in a small space with the same people for a long time. The ocean is silent, dark, and immense — and somewhere beneath it, a submarine moves quietly through the deep.

lines.text: ❌ "The submarine can to stay underwater for three months."

lines.text: Modal verbs (can, could, must, should, will) + bare infinitive — no 'to.' 'It can stay.' 'They must dive.' 'We should surface.' This rule has no exceptions. Even 'be able to' — which means the same as 'can' — follows a different structure: 'It is able to stay.'

lines.text: 'Tell' + person (no 'to'): 'He told the crew.' 'She told us.' 'Say' + to + person: 'He said to the crew.' Never 'told to the crew.' Remember: tell someone, say to someone.

lines.text: ✅ "How deep can the submarine go? Is it dangerous?"
lines.name: ✅ "How deep can the submarine go? Is it dangerous?"

lines.text: In questions with 'how + adjective/adverb', the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'How deep can it go?' 'How fast does it travel?' 'How long has it been underwater?' Never 'How deep it can go?' in a direct question (that word order is for indirect questions: 'I wonder how deep it can go').

lines.name: ❌ "The crew are working on the submarine since two months."

lines.text: ✅ "The crew have been working on the submarine for two months."

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for two months.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since January.' Also: use present perfect continuous ('have been working') for ongoing actions from past to present, not present simple ('are working').

lines.text: ❌ "There are less space on a submarine than on a ship."
lines.name: ❌ "There are less space on a submarine than on a ship."

lines.text: ✅ "There is less space on a submarine than on a ship."
lines.name: ✅ "There is less space on a submarine than on a ship."

lines.text: 'Space' (when meaning room/area) is uncountable: 'less space' with 'is.' 'Less' + uncountable, 'fewer' + countable: 'less space', 'fewer rooms.' The verb also changes: 'There is less space' (singular) vs. 'There are fewer rooms' (plural).

lines.text: A 'submarine' is a large, self-sufficient vessel that can operate independently for long periods. A 'submersible' is smaller and usually launched from a ship — used for research or deep-sea exploration. The Titan submersible disaster (2023) made this distinction widely known.

lines.text: Ships and submarines use specialised terms: 'port' (left side), 'starboard' (right side), 'bow' (front), 'stern' (back), 'hull' (body), 'galley' (kitchen), 'bridge' (control area on surface ships). A submarine's main control area is the 'conn' or 'control room'.

lines.text: Jules Verne's '20,000 Leagues Under the Sea' (1870) featured the fictional submarine Nautilus. 'The Hunt for Red October' (Tom Clancy) and 'Das Boot' (German film) are famous submarine stories. 'Yellow Submarine' is a Beatles song and animated film.

lines.text: 'Vessel' is the formal word for any ship or boat. Ships are traditionally referred to as 'she': 'She was launched in 1995.' Modern style guides now accept 'it'. 'HMS' = His/Her Majesty's Ship (Royal Navy). 'USS' = United States Ship.
